newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: COAL-FOR-GOLD SWAP ONE OPTION IN JCI/LONRHO TALKS.
newsitem.headline: COAL-FOR-GOLD SWAP ONE OPTION IN JCI/LONRHO TALKS.

text.p: South Africa's JCI Ltd and British conglomerate Lonrho PLC had enough mutual interests for future cooperation despite merger talks being called off on Monday, industry sources and analysts said.
JCI said it was discussing other ways to unlock value for the two firms' shareholders.
"The company confirms that it has been approached to discuss other possible transactions which could unlock value for shareholders in both JCI Ltd and Lonrho," JCI said in statement.
Industry sources said the companies would probably now explore asset swaps.

An industry source said one avenue that could be studied was swapping JCI's unlisted Tavistock coal division for Lonrho's 33.6 percent stake in Ashanti Goldfields Company Ltd -- one of the most succesful gold producers in Africa.
The source said most analysts would see Lonrho as being keen to acquire JCI's coal assets while JCI would want Lonrho's Ashanti stake.
"That would be a good suggestion," the source said.

Analysts said this could open the way for JCI to enter a deal with Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd in which JCI could swap the Ashanti stake for Anglo's stake in Lonrho, which the European Union has told it to reduce.
Anglo desperately wants a stake in Ghana's Ashanti and said last week that Lonrho had suggested swapping its stake in Ashanti for Anglo's Lonrho shares.
The South African mining giant has said a merger JCI/Lonrho would have its support but the company has stressed that it did not initiate the merger talks.
After pressure from the European Commission, Anglo said in April it would cut its 27 percent stake in Lonrho to less than 10 percent.
The EC said Anglo and Lonrho's combined platinum interests with that of another South African company, Gencor Ltd , would constitute a monopoly of the world platinum industry.
Lonrho holds substantial interest in two South African platinum mines.
Analysts said they believed the JCI/Lonrho talks, aimed at creating a global mining house with a market capitalisation of some $3 billion, were called off because JCI's price was too high.
"As the transaction went on, it became unrealistic. The deal floundered on price," Investec Securities analyst John Clemmow said.
He said with Lonrho trying to reorganise itself and dispose of its non-core hotel and African trading operations, its mining operations would be relatively small.
"When Lonrho Africa and the general trade division have gone, Lonrho mining will have a life that its nasty, brutish and short," he said, making it a prime takeover target.
